summary.text: Since residues \(1,9\pmod {10}\) are squares modulo \(5\), quadratic reciprocity makes \(5\) a square modulo \(p\); choosing a root \(x\) and setting \(n=x-1\) gives \(3\le n<p\) and \(p\mid n^2+2n-4\). Writing the continued-fraction numerator as \(N_2=n^2+2n-4=pq\), identities for its numerator recurrence show that \(q\) divides the companion denominator \(N_3\), while \(p\mid N_3\) would propagate through the recurrence to force \(p\mid4\); hence reduction cancels exactly \(q\) and leaves \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_2(n)=2-\frac3{3-\frac4{4-\frac5{\ddots-\frac{n-1}{(n-1)-n/(-4)}}}}
\]
be the expression inside the outer reciprocal in the definition of the sequence. Thus the continued fraction itself is \(1/R_2(n)\). We shall show that for every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\), one can choose \(n\ge3\) so that the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\) has absolute value \(p\). Since taking the reciprocal interchanges numerator and denominator, this says exactly that the reduced denominator of the continued fraction is \(p\), i.e. \(a(n)=p\).

For the tails of the expression, define
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=n-1+\frac n4,
\]
and, for \(2\le k\le n-2\), define recursively
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}.
\]
We first express these tails by integer continuants.

Define integers \(N_k=N_k(n)\) by
\[
N_n=4,\qquad N_{n-1}=5n-4,
\]
and, for \(2\le k\le n-2\),
\[
N_k=kN_{k+1}-(k+1)N_{k+2}. \tag{1}
\]
Then
\[
R_k(n)=\frac{N_k}{N_{k+1}}\qquad(2\le k\le n-1). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, at \(k=n-1\),
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=n-1+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4}=\frac{N_{n-1}}{N_n}.
\]
If (2) holds at \(k+1\), then
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{N_{k+1}/N_{k+2}}
      =\frac{kN_{k+1}-(k+1)N_{k+2}}{N_{k+1}}
      =\frac{N_k}{N_{k+1}},
\]
which proves the assertion by downward induction.

The relevant denominators in this calculation are nonzero. One convenient way to see this directly from the continued fraction is to prove, by downward induction, that
\[
R_k(n)\ge k-2\qquad(3\le k\le n-1). \tag{3}
\]
The assertion is immediate for \(k=n-1\), since
\(R_{n-1}=n-1+n/4>n-3\). If it holds at \(k+1\), where \(k\ge3\), then
\[
R_{k+1}\ge k-1>0.
\]
Moreover \((k+1)/(k-1)\le2\), so
\[
\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}\le2,
\qquad
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}\ge k-2.
\]
In particular \(R_3>0\) when \(n\ge4\). This also justifies the divisions occurring in the induction above and implies \(N_3\ne0\). When \(n=3\), one has \(N_3=4\), so again \(N_3\ne0\).

We next calculate \(N_2\). More generally, for every \(m\) with \(2\le m\le n-1\),
\[
N_2=(m-1)N_m-(m^2-2m)N_{m+1}. \tag{4}
\]
For \(m=2\) this is simply \(N_2=N_2\). If (4) holds for \(m\), substitute the recurrence
\[
N_m=mN_{m+1}-(m+1)N_{m+2}.
\]
The coefficient of \(N_{m+1}\) becomes
\[
m(m-1)-(m^2-2m)=m,
\]
and the coefficient of \(N_{m+2}\) becomes
\[
-(m-1)(m+1)=-(m^2-1).
\]
Thus
\[
N_2=mN_{m+1}-\bigl((m+1)^2-2(m+1)\bigr)N_{m+2},
\]
which is (4) with \(m+1\) in place of \(m\). This proves (4).

Taking \(m=n-1\) in (4), and using \(N_{n-1}=5n-4\) and \(N_n=4\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_2
&=(n-2)(5n-4)-\bigl((n-1)^2-2(n-1)\bigr)4\\
&=n^2+2n-4. \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently
\[
R_2(n)=\frac{n^2+2n-4}{N_3}. \tag{6}
\]
The fraction on the right need not yet be reduced; identifying precisely what cancels is the main point of the proof.

We record two divisibility consequences of the continuant recurrence.

First, suppose an integer \(m\) satisfies
\[
2\le m\le n-1\quad\text{and}\quad m\mid N_2.
\]
Putting this \(m\) into (4), and reducing modulo \(m\), gives
\[
N_2\equiv -N_m\pmod m,
\]
because \(m-1\equiv-1\pmod m\) and \(m^2-2m=m(m-2)\) is divisible by \(m\). Hence \(m\mid N_m\). The recurrence at \(m-1\) is
\[
N_{m-1}=(m-1)N_m-mN_{m+1},
\]
so \(m\mid N_{m-1}\) as well. Thereafter, if \(m\mid N_{k+1}\) and \(m\mid N_{k+2}\), recurrence (1) implies \(m\mid N_k\). Descending in this way yields
\[
m\mid N_k\qquad(2\le k\le m). \tag{7}
\]
In particular, if \(3\le m\le n-1\) and \(m\mid N_2\), then
\[
m\mid N_3. \tag{8}
\]

Second, let \(p\ge11\) be prime and suppose \(n<p\). Then \(p\) cannot divide both \(N_2\) and \(N_3\). More generally, if \(p\mid N_k\) and \(p\mid N_{k+1}\), recurrence (1) gives
\[
p\mid (k+1)N_{k+2}.
\]
For \(2\le k<n\), we have \(0<k+1\le n<p\), so \(p\nmid k+1\). Primality of \(p\) therefore implies \(p\mid N_{k+2}\). Beginning with \(N_2,N_3\), this propagates all the way to \(N_n\). But \(N_n=4\), which is not divisible by a prime \(p\ge11\). Therefore
\[
p\mid N_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\nmid N_3
\qquad\text{whenever }n<p. \tag{9}
\]

We now prove the key reduction statement. Suppose that
\[
n\ge3,
\qquad p\ge11\text{ is prime},
\qquad n<p,
\qquad p\mid N_2.
\]
Since (5) is positive for \(n\ge3\), write
\[
N_2=pq \tag{10}
\]
with \(q\) a positive integer.

We first note that \(q\ne2\). If \(q=2\), then by (5)
\[
n^2+2n-4=2p.
\]
The right side is even, and hence \(n^2\), and therefore \(n\), is even. Write \(n=2r\). Substitution gives
\[
2p=4r^2+4r-4=4(r^2+r-1),
\]
so \(p=2(r^2+r-1)\) is even. This is impossible because the prime \(p\ge11\) is odd. Thus
\[
q=1\quad\text{or}\quad q\ge3. \tag{11}
\]

We claim that in the second case \(q\le n-1\). Suppose instead that \(q\ge n\). If \(n\ge4\), then \(n<p\) gives \(p\ge n+1\), while (5) and (10) give
\[
qp=n^2+2n-4<n(n+2).
\]
Since \(q\ge n\), it follows that
\[
np\le qp<n(n+2),
\]
and hence \(p<n+2\). Thus the integer \(p\), lying between \(n+1\) and \(n+2\), must equal \(n+1\). But then
\[
qp=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5=p^2-5.
\]
The left side and \(p^2\) are divisible by \(p\), so \(p\mid5\), contradicting \(p\ge11\).

If \(n=3\), then (5) gives \(N_2=11\). A prime \(p\ge11\) dividing \(11\) must be \(11\), and then \(q=1\), contrary to the case \(q\ge3\). This proves that whenever \(q\ge3\),
\[
3\le q\le n-1. \tag{12}
\]

Now \(q\mid N_2\) by (10). If \(q=1\), it trivially divides \(N_3\). If \(q\ge3\), (12) and the divisibility propagation (8) show that it again divides \(N_3\). Therefore
\[
q\mid N_3. \tag{13}
\]

Let
\[
g=\gcd(|N_2|,|N_3|).
\]
By (10) and (13), \(q\mid g\), so write \(g=qh\) with \(h\ge1\). Since \(g\mid N_2=qp\), cancellation of the positive factor \(q\) shows that \(h\mid p\). As \(p\) is prime, either \(h=1\) or \(h=p\). The latter would imply \(p\mid g\), hence \(p\mid N_3\), contradicting (9), because we already have \(p\mid N_2\). Thus \(h=1\), and consequently
\[
\gcd(|N_2|,|N_3|)=q. \tag{14}
\]

It follows from (10), (14), and \(N_3\ne0\) that the numerator of the rational number \(N_2/N_3\), after reduction to lowest terms, has absolute value
\[
\frac{|N_2|}{\gcd(|N_2|,|N_3|)}
=\frac{pq}{q}=p. \tag{15}
\]
By (2), this rational number is \(R_2(n)\). Hence the reciprocal \(1/R_2(n)\), which is the continued fraction defining the sequence, has reduced denominator \(p\). We have therefore proved the following criterion:

> If \(p\ge11\) is prime, \(3\le n<p\), and
> \[
> p\mid n^2+2n-4,
> \]
> then \(a(n)=p\).

It remains to construct such an \(n\) for every prime in the stated congruence classes.

Let \(p\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\equiv1\quad\text{or}\quad9\pmod {10}.
\]
There is no prime less than \(11\) in either of these residue classes: among the nonnegative integers below \(11\), the only numbers congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) are \(1\) and \(9\), neither prime. Hence
\[
p\ge11. \tag{16}
\]
In particular, \(p\) is an odd prime distinct from \(5\).

Reducing the congruence modulo \(5\), we have
\[
p\equiv1\quad\text{or}\quad4\pmod5.
\]
Both residues are quadratic residues modulo \(5\): \(1\equiv1^2\pmod5\), and \(4\equiv2^2\pmod5\). Thus the Legendre symbol satisfies
\[
\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
Because \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity has no sign change here, and gives
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
Therefore there exists a residue \(x\pmod p\) satisfying
\[
x^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{17}
\]
Choose its standard representative with \(0\le x<p\).

In fact \(x\ge4\). For \(x=0,1,2,3\), the respective values of \(x^2-5\) are
\[
-5,-4,-1,4.
\]
None is divisible by the prime \(p\ge11\), contrary to (17). Hence
\[
4\le x<p. \tag{18}
\]
Set
\[
n=x-1.
\]
Then (18) gives \(n\ge3\) and \(n<p\). Moreover,
\[
n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5=x^2-5,
\]
which is divisible by \(p\) by (17). The criterion just proved therefore applies and yields
\[
a(n)=p.
\]

Thus every prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs as a term of A363347.
